{{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} (''Shoki''); {{ill|Mihotsuhime|WD=Q6378698|1=Mihotsuhime-no-Mikoto}}; {{ill|Tamakushi-hime|WD=Q11572681|1=Tamakushi-hime}}; {{ill|Yamatototohimomosohime no mikoto|WD=Q11387098|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}}| children = [[Himetataraisuzu-hime|Isukeyorihime / Isuzuhime]]
Kushimikata (''Kojiki'')
{{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} (''Nihon Shoki'') | texts = ''[[Kojiki]]'', ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', ''[[Fudoki|Harima Fudoki]]'' and others | gender = {{ill|male|WD=Q6581097|1=Male (gender)}} | offspring = {{ill|Himetataraisuzuhime|WD=Q5353793|1=Himetataraisuzu-hime}}; {{ill|Isuzu-yori Hime-no-mikoto|WD=Q10881557|1=Isuzuyori-hime}}; {{ill|Kamo no Kimi|WD=Q55809532|1=Kamo no Okimi}}; {{ill|Ōtataneko|WD=Q55536798|1=Ōtataneko}} | equivalent5_type = Japanese | equivalent5 = {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|WD=Q10940674|1=Ame no Wakahiko}}; {{ill|Honoakari|WD=Q60673696|1=Honoakari}}; {{ill|Honosusori|WD=Q10731395|1=Hosuseri}}; {{ill|Kotoshironushi|WD=Q8009611|1=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto}}; {{ill|Nigihayahi|WD=Q10949054|1=Nigihayahi}}; {{ill|Yamato no ōkuni tama no kami|WD=Q11387080|1=Yamato Okunitama}}; {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944|1=Ōkuninushi}} }} '''Ōmononushi''' ({{lang-ja|大物主神|Ōmononushi-no-Kami}}; {{ill|Historical kana orthography|en|Historical kana orthography|WD=Q1142552|lt=historical orthography|1=Historical kana orthography}}: ''Ohomononushi'') is a ''[[kami]]'' in [[Japanese mythology]] associated with {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} (also known as Mount Mimoro) in {{ill|Sakurai, Nara|en|Sakurai, Nara|WD=Q127026|lt=Sakurai|1=Sakurai, Nara}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}}. He is closely linked in the [[:en:Imperial house of Japan|imperial]] myth cycle recorded in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (ca. 712 CE) and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' (720 CE) with the earthly ''kami'' [[Ōkuninushi]] (Ōnamuchi); indeed, the latter text treats 'Ōmononushi' as another name for or an aspect - more precisely, the spirit or ''{{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=Mitama|1=Mitama}}'' - of Ōnamuchi. Ōmononushi's chief place of worship is [[:en:Ōmiwa jinja|Ōmiwa Shrine]] located at the foot of Mount Miwa, which serves as the shrine's object of worship (''[[shintai]]''); he is thus also known as '''Miwa-no-Ōkami''' ({{lang|ja|三輪大神}}, 'Great Deity of Miwa') or '''Miwa (Dai)myōjin''' ({{lang|ja|三輪(大)明神}}). In addition, he is also enshrined in some other shrines such as [[:ja:大杉神社|Ōsugi Shrine]] in {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|WD=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}. The deity of [[Kotohira-gū|Kotohira Shrine]] (''Kotohira-gū'') in {{ill|Kotohira, Kagawa|en|Kotohira, Kagawa|WD=Q1271483|lt=Kotohira|1=Kotohira, Kagawa}}, {{ill|Kagawa Prefecture|en|Kagawa Prefecture|WD=Q161454|lt=Kagawa Prefecture|1=Kagawa Prefecture}}, popularly known as '''[[Konpira Gongen|Konpira Daigongen]]''' ([[:ja:金毘羅大権現|金毘羅大権現]]), is also currently identified with Ōmononushi. ==Name== The name 'Ōmononushi' ({{Ruby|大物主|おおものぬし}}; {{ill|Historical kana orthography|en|Historical kana orthography|WD=Q1142552|lt=historical orthography|1=Historical kana orthography}}: おほものぬし, ''Ohomononushi''; {{ill|Old Japanese|en|Old Japanese|WD=Q5736700|lt=Old Japanese|1=Old Japanese}}: ''Opomo2no2nusi'') is translated either as 'Great Thing Master'{{cite book |author=Aston, William G. |date=1905 |title=Shinto (The Way of the Gods)|publisher=Longmans, Green & Co.|url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/46038/46038-h/46038-h.htm|page=276}}{{cite book |author=Cranston, Edwin A. |date=1998 |title=A Waka Anthology. Volume One: The Gem-Glistening Cup|publisher=Stanford University Press|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KqWjwalbmx4C&pg=PA72|page=72|isbn=9780804731577 }} (after a literal translation of the {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=characters|1=Kanji}} used in his name) or 'Great Spirit Master'{{cite journal |last1=Andreeva |first1=Anna |date=2007 |title=Saidaiji Monks and Esoteric Kami Worship at Ise and Miwa |url=https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/2911 |journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies |volume=34 |issue=2 |page=352 |access-date=2020-10-01}} (with ''mono'' being taken as meaning 'spirit' or 'supernatural entity'{{cite book |author=Nishimiya, Kazutami |date=2014 |title=Shinchō Nihon Koten Shūsei: Kojiki (新潮日本古典集成 古事記) |publisher=Shinchōsha}}). The deity is also given the name 'Yamato-no-Ōmononushi-Kushimikatama-no-Mikoto' (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命, lit. 'Great Master of Things / Spirits, the Wondrous Awe-Inspiring Spirit (''{{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=tama|1=Mitama}}'') of {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato|1=Yamato Province}}') in the ''Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko no Kanʼyogoto'' (Izumo Province 造神賀詞, 'Congratulatory Words of the Chieftain of Izumo'), a ritual declaration (''[[norito]]'') delivered by the governor or ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of {{ill|Izumo Province|en|Izumo Province|WD=Q582846|lt=Izumo Province|1=Izumo Province}} at the imperial court upon his appointment. A passage in the ''[[Fudoki]]'' of {{ill|Harima Province|en|Harima Province|WD=Q1047523|lt=Harima Province|1=Harima Province}} (modern {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}}) meanwhile refers to a deity worshiped at [[:ja:御坂神社|Misaka Shrine]] in the village of Shijimi in {{ill|Mino District, Hyōgo|en|Mino District, Hyōgo|WD=Q6868901|lt=Minō District|1=Mino District, Hyōgo}} (modern {{ill|Miki, Hyōgo|en|Miki, Hyōgo|WD=Q31238|lt=Miki City|1=Miki, Hyōgo}}) known both as 'Yatokakesu- / Yatokakasu-Mimoro-no-Mikoto' (八戸桂掛須御諸命) and 'Ōmononushi-Ashihara-no-Shiko(o)' (大物主葦原志許(乎); ''Ashihara-no-Shikoo'' 'Ugly Man / Young Warrior of the [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|Reed Plains]]' is used in the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Shoki'' as another name for Ōkuninushi).{{cite book |title=Harima Fudoki Shinkō (播磨風土記新考)|year=1931 |publisher=Ōokayama Shoten |author=Inoue, Michiyasu|pages=513–515|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N8f9JyeYcmEC&pg=PP543}}{{cite book |title=Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries |year=1997 |publisher=Association for Asian Studies, Inc. |translator=Aoki, Michiko Y.|page=231}} ==Mythology== [[File:Omiwa-jinja ootorii.JPG|thumb|left|290px|Mount Miwa with the ''[[torii]]'' of {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|en|Ōmiwa Shrine|WD=Q705542|lt=Ōmiwa Shrine|1=Ōmiwa Shrine}} in the foreground]] ===Ōmononushi and Ōkuninushi=== {{See also|Ōkuninushi}} Ōmononushi first appears in the narrative of the god Ōkuninushi's pacification and development of the terrestrial world, [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]]. When Ōkuninushi (also known as Ōnamuchi), the descendant (so the ''Kojiki'') or the son (''Nihon Shoki'') of the god [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]], took upon himself the monumental task of developing Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni, a dwarf named [[Sukunabikona]] appeared from beyond the sea and became his partner. However, after a time Sukunabikona left Ōkuninushi and went to the 'eternal land' (常世国, ''[[tokoyo no kuni]]''). As Ōkuninushi was lamenting Sukunabikona's departure, another god "illuminating the sea" appears before Ōkuninushi, promising to aid him in his task if he (Ōkuninushi) will worship him. Ōkuninushi, in accordance with the god's wish, then enshrined him in Mount Mimoro (Mount Miwa) in the land of {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato|1=Yamato Province}}.{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=115–117}}Chamberlain (1882). [https://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj035.htm Section XXVIII.—The August-Luck-Spirit-the-August-Wondrous-Spirit] While this god is yet unidentified at this point in the ''Kojiki'', the version of the myth found in the ''Nihon Shoki'' has this deity explicitly identify himself as Ōnamuchi's (the default name of Ōkuninushi in this text) {{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=''kushimitama'' and ''sakimitama''|1=Mitama}} ({{lang|ja|幸魂奇魂}}, 'wondrous spirit' and 'lucky/auspicious spirit', respectively).{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=61}} Indeed, this same passage lists 'Ōmononushi' as one of the various names for Ōnamuchi.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=59}} A variant version of the myth of Ōnamuchi's [[:en:Kuniyuzuri|cession of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]] to the gods of the heavenly realm [[Takamagahara]] found in the ''Shoki'' treats 'Ōmononushi' as a name for Ōnamuchi after he left the physical realm to govern the unseen world of the spirit. In this story, Ōnamuchi-as-Ōmononushi along with his son [[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi]] ascends to Takamagahara to swear fealty to the heavenly ''kami''. As a reward, the [[Kotoamatsukami|primordial deity]] [[Takamimusubi]] gives Ōmononushi his daughter Mihotsuhime (三穂津姫) to be his wife and then sends him back to earth with "the eighty myriads of deities" to become the guardians of the goddess [[Amaterasu]]'s descendants, the [[:en:Imperial house of Japan|Japanese imperial house]].{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book II |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=79–80}} In the ''Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko no Kanʼyogoto'', Ōnamochi (Ōkuninushi), after relinquishing his authority over the land, attaches his ''nigitama'' (和魂, 'gentle spirit') in an 'eight-hand {{ill|Bronze mirror|en|Bronze mirror|WD=Q1041984|lt=mirror|1=Bronze mirror}}' (八咫鏡 ''yata no kagami''), which he then enshrined in Miwa under the name 'Yamato-no-Ōmononushi-Kushimikatama-no-Mikoto' to serve as a patron of the imperial house along with his children, who he installed in various shrines in the Yamato area.{{cite book |author=Tsugita, Uruu |title=Norito Senmyō: Kōchū (祝詞宣命 校註) |date=1928|publisher=Meiji Shoin |pages=96–97|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1109286/56}} ===Isukeyorihime (Isuzuhime)=== [[File:Omiwa Shrine Worship Hall.jpg|280px|thumb|''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' of Ōmiwa Shrine]] The ''Kojiki'' relates that when Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko (also known as {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}), the great-grandson of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto|Ninigi]] (Amaterasu's grandson who [[Tenson kōrin|came down from heaven]] to govern Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni after it was surrendered by Ōkuninushi), was searching for a wife, he was told about a woman named [[:en:Seyadatarahime|Seyadatarahime]] (勢夜陀多良比売) who bore a daughter after she was impregnated by Ōmononushi, who took the form of a red arrow and struck her genitals while she was defecating in a ditch. Iwarebiko wooed this daughter, named Hototatara-Isusukihime (富登多多良伊須須岐比売) or Himetatara-Isukeyorihime (比売多多良伊須気余理比売; an altered form of the name which omits the [[taboo]] word ''hoto'' 'genitals'), and took her as his wife.{{cite book|author=R. A. B. Ponsonby-Fane|title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UVO4AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT412 |date=3 June 2014 |publisher=Taylor & Francis| isbn=978-1-136-89301-8|page=412}}{{cite web |last1=Kadoya |first1=Atsushi|title=Ōmononushi |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=126|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|accessdate=22 September 2015}} While the main narrative of the first volume of the ''Nihon Shoki'' first describes this daughter, there named [[Himetataraisuzu-hime|Himetatara-Isuzuhime]] (媛蹈鞴五十鈴媛), as the offspring of the god of Ōmiwa (i.e. Ōmononushi) in agreement with the ''Kojiki'', it is then immediately followed by an alternative account which portrays her as the child of the god Kotoshironushi and the goddess Mizokuhihime (溝樴姫) - also known as Tamakushihime (玉櫛姫) - conceived after Kotoshironushi transformed himself into a gigantic ''{{ill|Wani (dragon)|en|Wani (dragon)|WD=Q20049265|lt=wani|1=Wani (dragon)}}'' and had intercourse with her.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=61–62}} Likewise the main narrative in the third and fourth volumes refer to her as the daughter of Kotoshironushi rather than Ōmononushi.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book III |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=132}}{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book IV |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=138}} ===Ōtataneko and Ikuhi serve Ōmononushi=== Both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki'' relate that a series of devastating plagues affected the country during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}}. After performing {{ill|Futomani|en|Futomani|WD=Q5510530|lt=divination|1=Futomani}} to ascertain the will of the ''kami'', the emperor then received a revelation from Ōmononushi via a dream (''Kojiki'') or an {{ill|Oracle|en|Oracle|WD=Q217123|lt=Oracle|1=Oracle}} delivered by {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} (倭迹迹日百襲姫命), the emperor's grandaunt (''Shoki''). In it, Ōmononushi claimed responsibility for the pestilence and announced that it would not stop until he was offered due worship by a man named {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} (意富多多泥古命 / 大田田根子), who is either his son (''Shoki'') or his great-great-grandson (''Kojiki'') through a woman named Ikutamayorihime (活玉依毘売 / 活玉依媛). After {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} was found and appointed to serve Ōmononushi at his shrine, the epidemic ceased. {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} is reckoned to be the ancestor of the priestly clans of [[Kamo clan|Kamo]] (鴨君 ''Kamo no [[Kimi (kabane)|Kimi]]'') and [[Miwa clan|Miwa]] (神君 / 三輪君 ''Miwa no Kimi'').{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=201–202}}Chamberlain (1882). [https://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj071.htm Section LXIV.—Emperor Sū-jin (Part II.—A Pestilence Is Staid By Oho-tata-ne-ko)]{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book V |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspages=152-155}}{{cite book|title=Handbook of Contemporary Japanese Religions|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=of4yAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA85 |date=3 September 2012|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-23436-9|page=85}} The ''Shoki'' adds that Sujin appointed another individual named Ikuhi (活日) as the brewer of [[sake]] presented as offerings to Ōmononushi. When worship of the deity was conducted at the shrine in Miwa, Ikuhi offered the emperor some of this sacred sake ('''') while singing the following {{ill|Waka (mythology)|en|Waka (mythology)|WD=Q25205801|lt=song|1=Waka (mythology)}}: {{Verse translation | lang = Japanese | italicsoff = 1 | rtl1 = |''Kono miki wa''
''wa ga miki narazu''
''Yamato nasu''
''Ōmononushi no''
''kamishi miki''
''ikuhisa ikuhisa''{{cite book |editor1-last=Takeda |editor1-first=Yūkichi |title=Kiki Kayoshū (記紀歌謡集) |date=1948 |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1069683/63|pages=122–123}} |This sacred sake
Is not my sacred sake:
'Tis sacred sake brewed
By Oho-mono-nushi,
Of Yamato,
How long ago!
How long ago! | attr1 = | attr2 = Translation by [[:en:W. G. Aston|W. G. Aston]]}} A feast was then held at the shrine, after which the emperor sang: {{Verse translation | lang = Japanese | italicsoff = 1 | rtl1 = |''Umazake''
''Miwa no tono no''
''asato ni mo''
''oshi hirakane''
''Miwa no tonodo wo'' |The Hall of Miwa
⁠(Of sweet sake fame),
Even its morning-door
⁠I would push open—
The door of the Hall of Miwa. | attr1 = | attr2 = Translation by [[:en:W. G. Aston|W. G. Aston]]}} ===Affair with Ikutamayorihime=== The ''Kojiki'' follows the account of {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}}'s appointment as Ōmononushi's priest with the story of Ōmononushi's affair with Ikutamayorihime. The beautiful Ikutamayorihime was visited night after night by a handsome young stranger who got her with child. Anxious to discover the man's identity, Ikutamayorihime's parents advised her to sew a {{ill|Hemp|en|Hemp|WD=Q7150699|lt=Hemp|1=Hemp}} thread to the hem of the man's garment. The following morning, the yarn was found passing through the keyhole of her chamber door, leading straight to Mount Miwa. Ikutamayorihime and her parents accordingly knew that her lover had been Ōmononushi, the god of the mountain. This legend explains the name 'Miwa' as deriving from the three (''mi''-) loops or twists (''wa'') of hemp thread that remained.{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=203–204}}Chamberlain (1882). [https://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj072.htm Section LXV.—Emperor Sū-jin (PART III: Story of Oho-tata-ne-ko's Birth)]{{cite book|author=Carmen Blacker |title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MGeOAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA94|date=2 August 2004 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-31873-4|page=94}} ===Yamato-Totohimomosohime's death=== [[File:Hashihaka-kofun zenkei-2.jpg|thumb|310px|left|{{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} ([[:ja:箸墓古墳|箸墓古墳]]), a late 3rd-early 4th century Kofun (''[[kofun]]'') at the foot of Mount Miwa in Sakurai, Nara Prefecture. A legend recorded in the ''Nihon Shoki'' claims this tumulus to be the tomb of {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}}.]] The ''Nihon Shoki'' records the following story about {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}}, a daughter of {{ill|Emperor Kōrei|en|Emperor Kōrei|WD=Q313041|lt=Emperor Kōrei|1=Emperor Kōrei}} and Emperor Sujin's grandaunt. {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} became wed to Ōmononushi, but the god visited her only at night and was never seen in the daytime. When she requested to see his true form, he hid in her comb case, where she found him as a small snake. After her alarm caused the snake to flee in shame and anger to Mount Miwa, {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} in remorse stabs her genitals with a [[:en:Chopstick|Chopstick]] and dies.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book V |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspages=158-159}} This narrative serves as an {{ill|Origin myth|en|Origin myth|WD=Q390248|lt=Origin myth|1=Origin myth}} for {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} (''hashi (no) haka'' means 'chopstick tomb') at the western foot of Mount Miwa, which is here claimed to be {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime's|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} tomb. The tumulus, which the story claims to be made of stone from Mount Ōsaka (大坂山, identified with {{ill|Mount Nijō|en|Mount Nijō|WD=Q11371271|lt=Mount Nijō|1=Mount Nijō}} on the border of {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara|1=Nara Prefecture}} and {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka Prefecture}}, located 15.3 [[:en:Kilometers|Kilometers]] (9.5 [[:en:Miles|Miles]]) west of the tomb{{cite book |last1=Izumori |first1=Kō |title=Yamato no kofun o kataru (大和の古墳を語る) |date=1984 |publisher=Rokkō Shuppan |page=104}}), is said to have been made by men in the daytime and by the gods at night; the stones used in its construction are said to have been transported from the mountain to the mound by workers standing in single file, who passed the stones from hand to hand. ===Emperor Yūryaku and the serpent of Mount Miwa=== An episode recorded in the ''Shoki'' concerning {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} relates that the emperor, wishing to see the physical form of the god of Mount Miwa{{efn|A {{ill|Scholia|en|Scholia|WD=Q1358144|lt=Scholia|1=Scholia}} in the text remarks that the deity in question is identified either as Ōmononushi or as Uda-no-Sumisaka-no-Kami (菟田墨坂神, one of the deities worshiped by Emperor Sujin to quell the epidemic that occurred during his reign).{{cite web |last1=Mori |first1=Mizue |title=Udanosumisaka |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=160 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |accessdate=2020-10-07}}}} with his own eyes, commanded a retainer named Chiisakobe no Sugaru (少子部蜾蠃) to fetch the deity. Sugaru went up the mountain and captured a large snake, which he presented to the emperor. However, as Yūryaku neglected to ritually purify himself beforehand, the serpent made thunderous noise (or summoned {{ill|Thunder|en|Thunder|WD=Q83301|lt=Thunder|1=Thunder}}) and its eyeballs flashed. The emperor fled for fear of the snake and ordered it to be returned to Mount Miwa. He then gave the mountain (or Sugaru) the name 'Ikazuchi' (雷), meaning "thunder."{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book_XIV |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=347}} A different variant of this story is found in the ''[[Nihon Ryōiki]]'' (ca. 822 CE). There, Sugaru is commanded to capture the [[Raijin|thunder god]] after Sugaru accidentally walked into the palace while the emperor was making love with the empress. Sugaru then went out and summoned the god to appear before the emperor, at which lightning struck near the temple of Toyura-dera (modern {{ill|Kōgen-ji|en|Kōgen-ji|WD=Q11415914|lt=Kōgen-ji|1=Kōgen-ji}} in the {{ill|Asuka, Nara|en|Asuka, Nara|WD=Q752397|lt=village of Asuka|1=Asuka, Nara}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}}). Sugaru sent for priests to place this lightning (i.e. the thunder god) in a [[Mikoshi|palanquin]], which he then brought before the emperor. The emperor was frightened after the god gave off a brilliant flash of light and had it released at the hill where it fell, which became known as Ikazuchi-no-Oka (雷丘 'Thunder Hill').{{cite book |last1=Nakamura |first1=Kyoko Motomuchi |title=Miraculous Stories from the Japanese Buddhist Tradition: The Nihon Ryoiki of the Monk Kyokai |date=2013 |publisher=Routledge |pages=102–103 |isbn=9781136792533 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Oa3dAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA102}} ===In later mythology=== [[File:Eleven-faced Kannon Shorinji.JPG|thumb|200px|Late 8th century ({{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}) statue of the Eleven-faced {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara|1=Avalokiteśvara}} (''[[Kannon|Jūichimen Kannon]]''). Formerly the principal image or ''[[honzon]]'' of Daigorin-ji (the former ''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}'' of Ōmiwa Shrine), this image was transferred to [[:ja:聖林寺|Shorin-ji]] in Sakurai, Nara when [[Shinbutsu bunri|the separation of Shinto and Buddhism]] was mandated during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}.]] A late 13th century ({{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}) text, the ''Miwa Daimyōjin Engi'' (三輪大明神縁起), features retellings of two of the above myths concerning Ōmononushi reinterpreted within a Buddhist framework. *The ''Engi'''s version of the narrative of Ōnamuchi's encounter with Ōmononushi (based on the one found in the ''Nihon Shoki'') identifies the god enshrined in Miwa to be Tenshō Kōtaijin (天照皇太神, the [[Amaterasu]] of classical mythology). Indeed, Miwa Daimyōjin, the deity of Mount Miwa, and Kōtaijin, the deity of Mount Kamiji in {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|WD=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}} (i.e. [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]]), are treated in the text to be two different earthly incarnations of the same heavenly deity Tenshō / Amaterasu, who in turn is a [[Honji suijaku|manifestation]] of the {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha|1=Buddhahood}} {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Vairocana|1=Vairocana}} (Dainichi). At the same time, however, the text claims that the shrine in Miwa is superior to that of Ise, in that the Miwa deity's descent to earth occurred during the mythical [[:en:Kamiyo|Age of the Gods]], whereas Tenshō Daijin was only enshrined in Ise much later, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}}.{{cite journal |last1=Andreeva |first1=Anna |title=The Karmic Origins of the Great Bright Miwa Deity: A Transformation of the Sacred Mountain in Premodern Japan |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |date=2010 |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=245–296 |doi=10.1353/mni.2010.0003 |jstor=41303211 |s2cid=162818503 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41303211}} *The story of Ōmononushi's amorous relationship with Ikutamayorihime is here transformed into an origin legend of Daigorin-ji (大御輪寺, also Ōmiwa-dera), the Buddhist temple (''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}'') associated with Ōmiwa Shrine during the medieval period. {{Quote|This temple was the first Buddhist facility constructed in the ninety-ninth year of the reign of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}}, the eleventh human [sovereign]. At the time there was a certain Takeichihara ''{{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Dainagon|1=Dainagon}}'' (武一(二)原大納言). He had one daughter. The deity of this [Ōmiwa] shrine was secretly making his way every night to make love with this woman, who eventually bore a male child. Both the parents of the woman as well as all others [high and low] were suspicious and asked her the reason. The daughter, to resolve her own and others' suspicions, took a fine thread and attached it to the hem of [her lover's] garment, and sought to know where the thread led. It entered directly into the middle of the three places, the altar of the great shrine (''ōmiya no shadan'' 大宮之社壇). At that time they first learned that it was the Great Deity (''jinmyō'' 神明) [of Miwa]. Afterward, following a request of the ''dainagon'', the deity manifested itself in the form of a large snake and licked the prince's back (some legends say that it licked his chest). On the licked spot a golden mark appeared that said, "The Master of Great Things, of Upper First Rank, the Great Deity, Outstanding [for its services in the matters of state] (''shō ichii daimyōjin kun ittō Ōmono no nushi'' 正一位大明神勲一等大物之主)." [...] The ''dainagon'' retired from the world to his own mansion and converted his private residence into a Buddhist temple (''garan'' 伽藍). This was Ōmiwadera.}} :The narrative adds that the boy's mother died seven days after giving birth. The prince grew up, longing for his compassionate mother. To console the grieving boy, the Miwa deity appeared in the form of a man and gave him a statue bearing his mother's likeness. Thereafter, the prince constantly worshiped at the god's shrine until he reached his teens, when he secluded himself in a cell in the temple and entered ''[[:en:Samādhi|Samādhi]]'', never to come out again. Six centuries later, {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}} visited the temple and discovered the statue of the prince's mother, which the story identifies with the [[Honzon|principal image]] of Daigorin-ji, that of the Eleven-Faced [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara|1=Avalokiteśvara}}). Ōmononushi is the kami of rain. ==See also== *[[Ōkuninushi]] *{{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} *{{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=Mitama|1=Mitama}} *[[Kotohira-gū]] *{{ill|Snake worship|en|Snake worship|WD=Q3249489|lt=Snake worship|1=Snake worship}} *[[Kamo clan]] *[[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi]] *{{ill|Legend of the White Snake|en|Legend of the White Snake|WD=Q1329003|lt=Legend of the White Snake|1=Legend of the White Snake}} ==Notes== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Bibliography== *{{cite journal |last1=Andreeva |first1=Anna |title=The Karmic Origins of the Great Bright Miwa Deity: A Transformation of the Sacred Mountain in Premodern Japan |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |date=2010 |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=245–296 |doi=10.1353/mni.2010.0003 |jstor=41303211 |s2cid=162818503 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41303211}} *Aoki, Michiko Y., tr. (1997). ''Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries''. Association for Asian Studies, Inc. {{ISBN|978-0924304323}}. *Aston, William George, tr. (1896). ''Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697''. 2 vols. Kegan Paul. 1972 Tuttle reprint. *Chamberlain, Basil H., tr. (1919). [http://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/index.htm ''The Kojiki, Records of Ancient Matters'']. 1981 Tuttle reprint. *Philippi, Donald L. (2015). ''Kojiki''. Princeton University Press. {{ISBN|978-1400878000}}. ==External links== *[http://oomiwa.or.jp/ Official Website of Ōmiwa Shrine] (Japanese) *[http://oosugi-jinja.or.jp/ Official Website of Ōsugi Shrine] (Japanese) *[http://www.konpira.or.jp/ Official Website of Kotohira Shrine] (Japanese) {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{Kotohira Faith}} [[wikt:神酒#Etymology 2|miki]] [[en:Ōmononushi]] [[en:Ōmononushi]] {{Commons category|Ōmononushi}} [[fr:Ōmononushi]] [[ja:大物主]] [[mni:ꯑꯣꯃꯣꯅꯣꯅꯨꯁꯤ]] [[ru:Омононуси]] [[simple:Ōmononushi]] [[zh:大物主]] {{wikidata link|Q10936701}} [[Category:Agricultural deities]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Pages with simple english wikipedia interwikis]] [[Category:Shinto]] [[Category:Shinto kami]] [[Category:Snake gods]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[Category:pages]]

Kushimikata (''Kojiki'')
{{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} (''Nihon Shoki'') | texts = ''[[Kojiki]]'', ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', ''[[Fudoki|Harima Fudoki]]'' and others | gender = {{ill|male|WD=Q6581097|1=Male (gender)}} | offspring = {{ill|Himetataraisuzuhime|WD=Q5353793|1=Himetataraisuzu-hime}}; {{ill|Isuzu-yori Hime-no-mikoto|WD=Q10881557|1=Isuzuyori-hime}}; {{ill|Kamo no Kimi|WD=Q55809532|1=Kamo no Okimi}}; {{ill|Ōtataneko|WD=Q55536798|1=Ōtataneko}} | equivalent5_type = Japanese | equivalent5 = {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|WD=Q10940674|1=Ame no Wakahiko}}; {{ill|Honoakari|WD=Q60673696|1=Honoakari}}; {{ill|Honosusori|WD=Q10731395|1=Hosuseri}}; {{ill|Kotoshironushi|WD=Q8009611|1=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto}}; {{ill|Nigihayahi|WD=Q10949054|1=Nigihayahi}}; {{ill|Yamato no ōkuni tama no kami|WD=Q11387080|1=Yamato Okunitama}}; {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944|1=Ōkuninushi}} }} '''Ōmononushi''' ({{lang-ja|大物主神|Ōmononushi-no-Kami}}; {{ill|Historical kana orthography|en|Historical kana orthography|WD=Q1142552|lt=historical orthography|1=Historical kana orthography}}: ''Ohomononushi'') is a ''[[kami]]'' in [[Japanese mythology]] associated with {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} (also known as Mount Mimoro) in {{ill|Sakurai, Nara|en|Sakurai, Nara|WD=Q127026|lt=Sakurai|1=Sakurai, Nara}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}}. He is closely linked in the [[:en:Imperial house of Japan|imperial]] myth cycle recorded in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (ca. 712 CE) and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' (720 CE) with the earthly ''kami'' [[Ōkuninushi]] (Ōnamuchi); indeed, the latter text treats 'Ōmononushi' as another name for or an aspect - more precisely, the spirit or ''{{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=Mitama|1=Mitama}}'' - of Ōnamuchi. Ōmononushi's chief place of worship is [[:en:Ōmiwa jinja|Ōmiwa Shrine]] located at the foot of Mount Miwa, which serves as the shrine's object of worship (''[[shintai]]''); he is thus also known as '''Miwa-no-Ōkami''' ({{lang|ja|三輪大神}}, 'Great Deity of Miwa') or '''Miwa (Dai)myōjin''' ({{lang|ja|三輪(大)明神}}). In addition, he is also enshrined in some other shrines such as [[:ja:大杉神社|Ōsugi Shrine]] in {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|WD=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}. The deity of [[Kotohira-gū|Kotohira Shrine]] (''Kotohira-gū'') in {{ill|Kotohira, Kagawa|en|Kotohira, Kagawa|WD=Q1271483|lt=Kotohira|1=Kotohira, Kagawa}}, {{ill|Kagawa Prefecture|en|Kagawa Prefecture|WD=Q161454|lt=Kagawa Prefecture|1=Kagawa Prefecture}}, popularly known as '''[[Konpira Gongen|Konpira Daigongen]]''' ([[:ja:金毘羅大権現|金毘羅大権現]]), is also currently identified with Ōmononushi. ==Name== The name 'Ōmononushi' ({{Ruby|大物主|おおものぬし}}; {{ill|Historical kana orthography|en|Historical kana orthography|WD=Q1142552|lt=historical orthography|1=Historical kana orthography}}: おほものぬし, ''Ohomononushi''; {{ill|Old Japanese|en|Old Japanese|WD=Q5736700|lt=Old Japanese|1=Old Japanese}}: ''Opomo2no2nusi'') is translated either as 'Great Thing Master'{{cite book |author=Aston, William G. |date=1905 |title=Shinto (The Way of the Gods)|publisher=Longmans, Green & Co.|url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/46038/46038-h/46038-h.htm|page=276}}{{cite book |author=Cranston, Edwin A. |date=1998 |title=A Waka Anthology. Volume One: The Gem-Glistening Cup|publisher=Stanford University Press|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KqWjwalbmx4C&pg=PA72|page=72|isbn=9780804731577 }} (after a literal translation of the {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=characters|1=Kanji}} used in his name) or 'Great Spirit Master'{{cite journal |last1=Andreeva |first1=Anna |date=2007 |title=Saidaiji Monks and Esoteric Kami Worship at Ise and Miwa |url=https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/2911 |journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies |volume=34 |issue=2 |page=352 |access-date=2020-10-01}} (with ''mono'' being taken as meaning 'spirit' or 'supernatural entity'{{cite book |author=Nishimiya, Kazutami |date=2014 |title=Shinchō Nihon Koten Shūsei: Kojiki (新潮日本古典集成 古事記) |publisher=Shinchōsha}}). The deity is also given the name 'Yamato-no-Ōmononushi-Kushimikatama-no-Mikoto' (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命, lit. 'Great Master of Things / Spirits, the Wondrous Awe-Inspiring Spirit (''{{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=tama|1=Mitama}}'') of {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato|1=Yamato Province}}') in the ''Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko no Kanʼyogoto'' (Izumo Province 造神賀詞, 'Congratulatory Words of the Chieftain of Izumo'), a ritual declaration (''[[norito]]'') delivered by the governor or ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of {{ill|Izumo Province|en|Izumo Province|WD=Q582846|lt=Izumo Province|1=Izumo Province}} at the imperial court upon his appointment. A passage in the ''[[Fudoki]]'' of {{ill|Harima Province|en|Harima Province|WD=Q1047523|lt=Harima Province|1=Harima Province}} (modern {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}}) meanwhile refers to a deity worshiped at [[:ja:御坂神社|Misaka Shrine]] in the village of Shijimi in {{ill|Mino District, Hyōgo|en|Mino District, Hyōgo|WD=Q6868901|lt=Minō District|1=Mino District, Hyōgo}} (modern {{ill|Miki, Hyōgo|en|Miki, Hyōgo|WD=Q31238|lt=Miki City|1=Miki, Hyōgo}}) known both as 'Yatokakesu- / Yatokakasu-Mimoro-no-Mikoto' (八戸桂掛須御諸命) and 'Ōmononushi-Ashihara-no-Shiko(o)' (大物主葦原志許(乎); ''Ashihara-no-Shikoo'' 'Ugly Man / Young Warrior of the [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|Reed Plains]]' is used in the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Shoki'' as another name for Ōkuninushi).{{cite book |title=Harima Fudoki Shinkō (播磨風土記新考)|year=1931 |publisher=Ōokayama Shoten |author=Inoue, Michiyasu|pages=513–515|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N8f9JyeYcmEC&pg=PP543}}{{cite book |title=Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries |year=1997 |publisher=Association for Asian Studies, Inc. |translator=Aoki, Michiko Y.|page=231}} ==Mythology== [[File:Omiwa-jinja ootorii.JPG|thumb|left|290px|Mount Miwa with the ''[[torii]]'' of {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|en|Ōmiwa Shrine|WD=Q705542|lt=Ōmiwa Shrine|1=Ōmiwa Shrine}} in the foreground]] ===Ōmononushi and Ōkuninushi=== {{See also|Ōkuninushi}} Ōmononushi first appears in the narrative of the god Ōkuninushi's pacification and development of the terrestrial world, [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]]. When Ōkuninushi (also known as Ōnamuchi), the descendant (so the ''Kojiki'') or the son (''Nihon Shoki'') of the god [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]], took upon himself the monumental task of developing Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni, a dwarf named [[Sukunabikona]] appeared from beyond the sea and became his partner. However, after a time Sukunabikona left Ōkuninushi and went to the 'eternal land' (常世国, ''[[tokoyo no kuni]]''). As Ōkuninushi was lamenting Sukunabikona's departure, another god "illuminating the sea" appears before Ōkuninushi, promising to aid him in his task if he (Ōkuninushi) will worship him. Ōkuninushi, in accordance with the god's wish, then enshrined him in Mount Mimoro (Mount Miwa) in the land of {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato|1=Yamato Province}}.{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=115–117}}Chamberlain (1882). [https://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj035.htm Section XXVIII.—The August-Luck-Spirit-the-August-Wondrous-Spirit] While this god is yet unidentified at this point in the ''Kojiki'', the version of the myth found in the ''Nihon Shoki'' has this deity explicitly identify himself as Ōnamuchi's (the default name of Ōkuninushi in this text) {{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=''kushimitama'' and ''sakimitama''|1=Mitama}} ({{lang|ja|幸魂奇魂}}, 'wondrous spirit' and 'lucky/auspicious spirit', respectively).{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=61}} Indeed, this same passage lists 'Ōmononushi' as one of the various names for Ōnamuchi.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=59}} A variant version of the myth of Ōnamuchi's [[:en:Kuniyuzuri|cession of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]] to the gods of the heavenly realm [[Takamagahara]] found in the ''Shoki'' treats 'Ōmononushi' as a name for Ōnamuchi after he left the physical realm to govern the unseen world of the spirit. In this story, Ōnamuchi-as-Ōmononushi along with his son [[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi]] ascends to Takamagahara to swear fealty to the heavenly ''kami''. As a reward, the [[Kotoamatsukami|primordial deity]] [[Takamimusubi]] gives Ōmononushi his daughter Mihotsuhime (三穂津姫) to be his wife and then sends him back to earth with "the eighty myriads of deities" to become the guardians of the goddess [[Amaterasu]]'s descendants, the [[:en:Imperial house of Japan|Japanese imperial house]].{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book II |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=79–80}} In the ''Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko no Kanʼyogoto'', Ōnamochi (Ōkuninushi), after relinquishing his authority over the land, attaches his ''nigitama'' (和魂, 'gentle spirit') in an 'eight-hand {{ill|Bronze mirror|en|Bronze mirror|WD=Q1041984|lt=mirror|1=Bronze mirror}}' (八咫鏡 ''yata no kagami''), which he then enshrined in Miwa under the name 'Yamato-no-Ōmononushi-Kushimikatama-no-Mikoto' to serve as a patron of the imperial house along with his children, who he installed in various shrines in the Yamato area.{{cite book |author=Tsugita, Uruu |title=Norito Senmyō: Kōchū (祝詞宣命 校註) |date=1928|publisher=Meiji Shoin |pages=96–97|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1109286/56}} ===Isukeyorihime (Isuzuhime)=== [[File:Omiwa Shrine Worship Hall.jpg|280px|thumb|''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' of Ōmiwa Shrine]] The ''Kojiki'' relates that when Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko (also known as {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}), the great-grandson of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto|Ninigi]] (Amaterasu's grandson who [[Tenson kōrin|came down from heaven]] to govern Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni after it was surrendered by Ōkuninushi), was searching for a wife, he was told about a woman named [[:en:Seyadatarahime|Seyadatarahime]] (勢夜陀多良比売) who bore a daughter after she was impregnated by Ōmononushi, who took the form of a red arrow and struck her genitals while she was defecating in a ditch. Iwarebiko wooed this daughter, named Hototatara-Isusukihime (富登多多良伊須須岐比売) or Himetatara-Isukeyorihime (比売多多良伊須気余理比売; an altered form of the name which omits the [[taboo]] word ''hoto'' 'genitals'), and took her as his wife.{{cite book|author=R. A. B. Ponsonby-Fane|title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UVO4AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT412 |date=3 June 2014 |publisher=Taylor & Francis| isbn=978-1-136-89301-8|page=412}}{{cite web |last1=Kadoya |first1=Atsushi|title=Ōmononushi |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=126|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|accessdate=22 September 2015}} While the main narrative of the first volume of the ''Nihon Shoki'' first describes this daughter, there named [[Himetataraisuzu-hime|Himetatara-Isuzuhime]] (媛蹈鞴五十鈴媛), as the offspring of the god of Ōmiwa (i.e. Ōmononushi) in agreement with the ''Kojiki'', it is then immediately followed by an alternative account which portrays her as the child of the god Kotoshironushi and the goddess Mizokuhihime (溝樴姫) - also known as Tamakushihime (玉櫛姫) - conceived after Kotoshironushi transformed himself into a gigantic ''{{ill|Wani (dragon)|en|Wani (dragon)|WD=Q20049265|lt=wani|1=Wani (dragon)}}'' and had intercourse with her.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=61–62}} Likewise the main narrative in the third and fourth volumes refer to her as the daughter of Kotoshironushi rather than Ōmononushi.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book III |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=132}}{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book IV |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=138}} ===Ōtataneko and Ikuhi serve Ōmononushi=== Both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki'' relate that a series of devastating plagues affected the country during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}}. After performing {{ill|Futomani|en|Futomani|WD=Q5510530|lt=divination|1=Futomani}} to ascertain the will of the ''kami'', the emperor then received a revelation from Ōmononushi via a dream (''Kojiki'') or an {{ill|Oracle|en|Oracle|WD=Q217123|lt=Oracle|1=Oracle}} delivered by {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} (倭迹迹日百襲姫命), the emperor's grandaunt (''Shoki''). In it, Ōmononushi claimed responsibility for the pestilence and announced that it would not stop until he was offered due worship by a man named {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} (意富多多泥古命 / 大田田根子), who is either his son (''Shoki'') or his great-great-grandson (''Kojiki'') through a woman named Ikutamayorihime (活玉依毘売 / 活玉依媛). After {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} was found and appointed to serve Ōmononushi at his shrine, the epidemic ceased. {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}} is reckoned to be the ancestor of the priestly clans of [[Kamo clan|Kamo]] (鴨君 ''Kamo no [[Kimi (kabane)|Kimi]]'') and [[Miwa clan|Miwa]] (神君 / 三輪君 ''Miwa no Kimi'').{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=201–202}}Chamberlain (1882). [https://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj071.htm Section LXIV.—Emperor Sū-jin (Part II.—A Pestilence Is Staid By Oho-tata-ne-ko)]{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book V |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspages=152-155}}{{cite book|title=Handbook of Contemporary Japanese Religions|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=of4yAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA85 |date=3 September 2012|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-23436-9|page=85}} The ''Shoki'' adds that Sujin appointed another individual named Ikuhi (活日) as the brewer of [[sake]] presented as offerings to Ōmononushi. When worship of the deity was conducted at the shrine in Miwa, Ikuhi offered the emperor some of this sacred sake ('''') while singing the following {{ill|Waka (mythology)|en|Waka (mythology)|WD=Q25205801|lt=song|1=Waka (mythology)}}: {{Verse translation | lang = Japanese | italicsoff = 1 | rtl1 = |''Kono miki wa''
''wa ga miki narazu''
''Yamato nasu''
''Ōmononushi no''
''kamishi miki''
''ikuhisa ikuhisa''{{cite book |editor1-last=Takeda |editor1-first=Yūkichi |title=Kiki Kayoshū (記紀歌謡集) |date=1948 |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1069683/63|pages=122–123}} |This sacred sake
Is not my sacred sake:
'Tis sacred sake brewed
By Oho-mono-nushi,
Of Yamato,
How long ago!
How long ago! | attr1 = | attr2 = Translation by [[:en:W. G. Aston|W. G. Aston]]}} A feast was then held at the shrine, after which the emperor sang: {{Verse translation | lang = Japanese | italicsoff = 1 | rtl1 = |''Umazake''
''Miwa no tono no''
''asato ni mo''
''oshi hirakane''
''Miwa no tonodo wo'' |The Hall of Miwa
⁠(Of sweet sake fame),
Even its morning-door
⁠I would push open—
The door of the Hall of Miwa. | attr1 = | attr2 = Translation by [[:en:W. G. Aston|W. G. Aston]]}} ===Affair with Ikutamayorihime=== The ''Kojiki'' follows the account of {{ill|Ōtataneko|ja|大田田根子|1=Ōtataneko|4=fr|5=Ōtataneko命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtataneko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to FR}}'s appointment as Ōmononushi's priest with the story of Ōmononushi's affair with Ikutamayorihime. The beautiful Ikutamayorihime was visited night after night by a handsome young stranger who got her with child. Anxious to discover the man's identity, Ikutamayorihime's parents advised her to sew a {{ill|Hemp|en|Hemp|WD=Q7150699|lt=Hemp|1=Hemp}} thread to the hem of the man's garment. The following morning, the yarn was found passing through the keyhole of her chamber door, leading straight to Mount Miwa. Ikutamayorihime and her parents accordingly knew that her lover had been Ōmononushi, the god of the mountain. This legend explains the name 'Miwa' as deriving from the three (''mi''-) loops or twists (''wa'') of hemp thread that remained.{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=203–204}}Chamberlain (1882). [https://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj072.htm Section LXV.—Emperor Sū-jin (PART III: Story of Oho-tata-ne-ko's Birth)]{{cite book|author=Carmen Blacker |title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MGeOAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA94|date=2 August 2004 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-31873-4|page=94}} ===Yamato-Totohimomosohime's death=== [[File:Hashihaka-kofun zenkei-2.jpg|thumb|310px|left|{{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} ([[:ja:箸墓古墳|箸墓古墳]]), a late 3rd-early 4th century Kofun (''[[kofun]]'') at the foot of Mount Miwa in Sakurai, Nara Prefecture. A legend recorded in the ''Nihon Shoki'' claims this tumulus to be the tomb of {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}}.]] The ''Nihon Shoki'' records the following story about {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}}, a daughter of {{ill|Emperor Kōrei|en|Emperor Kōrei|WD=Q313041|lt=Emperor Kōrei|1=Emperor Kōrei}} and Emperor Sujin's grandaunt. {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} became wed to Ōmononushi, but the god visited her only at night and was never seen in the daytime. When she requested to see his true form, he hid in her comb case, where she found him as a small snake. After her alarm caused the snake to flee in shame and anger to Mount Miwa, {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} in remorse stabs her genitals with a [[:en:Chopstick|Chopstick]] and dies.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book V |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspages=158-159}} This narrative serves as an {{ill|Origin myth|en|Origin myth|WD=Q390248|lt=Origin myth|1=Origin myth}} for {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} (''hashi (no) haka'' means 'chopstick tomb') at the western foot of Mount Miwa, which is here claimed to be {{ill|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|en|Princess Yamato Totohi Momoso|WD=Q11387098|lt=Yamato-Totohimomosohime's|1=Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime}} tomb. The tumulus, which the story claims to be made of stone from Mount Ōsaka (大坂山, identified with {{ill|Mount Nijō|en|Mount Nijō|WD=Q11371271|lt=Mount Nijō|1=Mount Nijō}} on the border of {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara|1=Nara Prefecture}} and {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka Prefecture}}, located 15.3 [[:en:Kilometers|Kilometers]] (9.5 [[:en:Miles|Miles]]) west of the tomb{{cite book |last1=Izumori |first1=Kō |title=Yamato no kofun o kataru (大和の古墳を語る) |date=1984 |publisher=Rokkō Shuppan |page=104}}), is said to have been made by men in the daytime and by the gods at night; the stones used in its construction are said to have been transported from the mountain to the mound by workers standing in single file, who passed the stones from hand to hand. ===Emperor Yūryaku and the serpent of Mount Miwa=== An episode recorded in the ''Shoki'' concerning {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} relates that the emperor, wishing to see the physical form of the god of Mount Miwa{{efn|A {{ill|Scholia|en|Scholia|WD=Q1358144|lt=Scholia|1=Scholia}} in the text remarks that the deity in question is identified either as Ōmononushi or as Uda-no-Sumisaka-no-Kami (菟田墨坂神, one of the deities worshiped by Emperor Sujin to quell the epidemic that occurred during his reign).{{cite web |last1=Mori |first1=Mizue |title=Udanosumisaka |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=160 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |accessdate=2020-10-07}}}} with his own eyes, commanded a retainer named Chiisakobe no Sugaru (少子部蜾蠃) to fetch the deity. Sugaru went up the mountain and captured a large snake, which he presented to the emperor. However, as Yūryaku neglected to ritually purify himself beforehand, the serpent made thunderous noise (or summoned {{ill|Thunder|en|Thunder|WD=Q83301|lt=Thunder|1=Thunder}}) and its eyeballs flashed. The emperor fled for fear of the snake and ordered it to be returned to Mount Miwa. He then gave the mountain (or Sugaru) the name 'Ikazuchi' (雷), meaning "thunder."{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book_XIV |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=347}} A different variant of this story is found in the ''[[Nihon Ryōiki]]'' (ca. 822 CE). There, Sugaru is commanded to capture the [[Raijin|thunder god]] after Sugaru accidentally walked into the palace while the emperor was making love with the empress. Sugaru then went out and summoned the god to appear before the emperor, at which lightning struck near the temple of Toyura-dera (modern {{ill|Kōgen-ji|en|Kōgen-ji|WD=Q11415914|lt=Kōgen-ji|1=Kōgen-ji}} in the {{ill|Asuka, Nara|en|Asuka, Nara|WD=Q752397|lt=village of Asuka|1=Asuka, Nara}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}}). Sugaru sent for priests to place this lightning (i.e. the thunder god) in a [[Mikoshi|palanquin]], which he then brought before the emperor. The emperor was frightened after the god gave off a brilliant flash of light and had it released at the hill where it fell, which became known as Ikazuchi-no-Oka (雷丘 'Thunder Hill').{{cite book |last1=Nakamura |first1=Kyoko Motomuchi |title=Miraculous Stories from the Japanese Buddhist Tradition: The Nihon Ryoiki of the Monk Kyokai |date=2013 |publisher=Routledge |pages=102–103 |isbn=9781136792533 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Oa3dAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA102}} ===In later mythology=== [[File:Eleven-faced Kannon Shorinji.JPG|thumb|200px|Late 8th century ({{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}) statue of the Eleven-faced {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara|1=Avalokiteśvara}} (''[[Kannon|Jūichimen Kannon]]''). Formerly the principal image or ''[[honzon]]'' of Daigorin-ji (the former ''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}'' of Ōmiwa Shrine), this image was transferred to [[:ja:聖林寺|Shorin-ji]] in Sakurai, Nara when [[Shinbutsu bunri|the separation of Shinto and Buddhism]] was mandated during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}.]] A late 13th century ({{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}) text, the ''Miwa Daimyōjin Engi'' (三輪大明神縁起), features retellings of two of the above myths concerning Ōmononushi reinterpreted within a Buddhist framework. *The ''Engi'''s version of the narrative of Ōnamuchi's encounter with Ōmononushi (based on the one found in the ''Nihon Shoki'') identifies the god enshrined in Miwa to be Tenshō Kōtaijin (天照皇太神, the [[Amaterasu]] of classical mythology). Indeed, Miwa Daimyōjin, the deity of Mount Miwa, and Kōtaijin, the deity of Mount Kamiji in {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|WD=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}} (i.e. [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]]), are treated in the text to be two different earthly incarnations of the same heavenly deity Tenshō / Amaterasu, who in turn is a [[Honji suijaku|manifestation]] of the {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha|1=Buddhahood}} {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Vairocana|1=Vairocana}} (Dainichi). At the same time, however, the text claims that the shrine in Miwa is superior to that of Ise, in that the Miwa deity's descent to earth occurred during the mythical [[:en:Kamiyo|Age of the Gods]], whereas Tenshō Daijin was only enshrined in Ise much later, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}}.{{cite journal |last1=Andreeva |first1=Anna |title=The Karmic Origins of the Great Bright Miwa Deity: A Transformation of the Sacred Mountain in Premodern Japan |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |date=2010 |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=245–296 |doi=10.1353/mni.2010.0003 |jstor=41303211 |s2cid=162818503 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41303211}} *The story of Ōmononushi's amorous relationship with Ikutamayorihime is here transformed into an origin legend of Daigorin-ji (大御輪寺, also Ōmiwa-dera), the Buddhist temple (''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}'') associated with Ōmiwa Shrine during the medieval period. {{Quote|This temple was the first Buddhist facility constructed in the ninety-ninth year of the reign of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}}, the eleventh human [sovereign]. At the time there was a certain Takeichihara ''{{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Dainagon|1=Dainagon}}'' (武一(二)原大納言). He had one daughter. The deity of this [Ōmiwa] shrine was secretly making his way every night to make love with this woman, who eventually bore a male child. Both the parents of the woman as well as all others [high and low] were suspicious and asked her the reason. The daughter, to resolve her own and others' suspicions, took a fine thread and attached it to the hem of [her lover's] garment, and sought to know where the thread led. It entered directly into the middle of the three places, the altar of the great shrine (''ōmiya no shadan'' 大宮之社壇). At that time they first learned that it was the Great Deity (''jinmyō'' 神明) [of Miwa]. Afterward, following a request of the ''dainagon'', the deity manifested itself in the form of a large snake and licked the prince's back (some legends say that it licked his chest). On the licked spot a golden mark appeared that said, "The Master of Great Things, of Upper First Rank, the Great Deity, Outstanding [for its services in the matters of state] (''shō ichii daimyōjin kun ittō Ōmono no nushi'' 正一位大明神勲一等大物之主)." [...] The ''dainagon'' retired from the world to his own mansion and converted his private residence into a Buddhist temple (''garan'' 伽藍). This was Ōmiwadera.}} :The narrative adds that the boy's mother died seven days after giving birth. The prince grew up, longing for his compassionate mother. To console the grieving boy, the Miwa deity appeared in the form of a man and gave him a statue bearing his mother's likeness. Thereafter, the prince constantly worshiped at the god's shrine until he reached his teens, when he secluded himself in a cell in the temple and entered ''[[:en:Samādhi|Samādhi]]'', never to come out again. Six centuries later, {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}} visited the temple and discovered the statue of the prince's mother, which the story identifies with the [[Honzon|principal image]] of Daigorin-ji, that of the Eleven-Faced [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara|1=Avalokiteśvara}}). Ōmononushi is the kami of rain. ==See also== *[[Ōkuninushi]] *{{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} *{{ill|Mitama|en|Mitama|WD=Q495568|lt=Mitama|1=Mitama}} *[[Kotohira-gū]] *{{ill|Snake worship|en|Snake worship|WD=Q3249489|lt=Snake worship|1=Snake worship}} *[[Kamo clan]] *[[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi]] *{{ill|Legend of the White Snake|en|Legend of the White Snake|WD=Q1329003|lt=Legend of the White Snake|1=Legend of the White Snake}} ==Notes== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Bibliography== *{{cite journal |last1=Andreeva |first1=Anna |title=The Karmic Origins of the Great Bright Miwa Deity: A Transformation of the Sacred Mountain in Premodern Japan |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |date=2010 |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=245–296 |doi=10.1353/mni.2010.0003 |jstor=41303211 |s2cid=162818503 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41303211}} *Aoki, Michiko Y., tr. (1997). ''Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries''. Association for Asian Studies, Inc. {{ISBN|978-0924304323}}. *Aston, William George, tr. (1896). ''Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697''. 2 vols. Kegan Paul. 1972 Tuttle reprint. *Chamberlain, Basil H., tr. (1919). [http://www.sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/index.htm ''The Kojiki, Records of Ancient Matters'']. 1981 Tuttle reprint. *Philippi, Donald L. (2015). ''Kojiki''. Princeton University Press. {{ISBN|978-1400878000}}. ==External links== *[http://oomiwa.or.jp/ Official Website of Ōmiwa Shrine] (Japanese) *[http://oosugi-jinja.or.jp/ Official Website of Ōsugi Shrine] (Japanese) *[http://www.konpira.or.jp/ Official Website of Kotohira Shrine] (Japanese) {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{Kotohira Faith}} [[wikt:神酒#Etymology 2|miki]] [[en:Ōmononushi]] [[en:Ōmononushi]] {{Commons category|Ōmononushi}} [[fr:Ōmononushi]] [[ja:大物主]] [[mni:ꯑꯣꯃꯣꯅꯣꯅꯨꯁꯤ]] [[ru:Омононуси]] [[simple:Ōmononushi]] [[zh:大物主]] {{wikidata link|Q10936701}} [[Category:Agricultural deities]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Pages with simple english wikipedia interwikis]] [[Category:Shinto]] [[Category:Shinto kami]] [[Category:Snake gods]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]]
